title: Principal Component Analysis (PCA)
abstract:
PCA transforms high-dimensional data into lower-dimensional data while keeping
the essence of the data. This document builds it from the ground up: the notes'
room-and-washroom intuition for why feature extraction is needed when
selection cannot choose, the variance-maximisation objective, the full
derivation via Lagrange multipliers to the eigenvalue problem, the covariance
matrix and its eigendecomposition, the SVD route that libraries actually use,
explained variance and the scree plot, why scaling is mandatory, from-scratch
code verified against scikit-learn, and the cases where PCA is the wrong tool.

blocks.t: What PCA Is
From the notes

items: Unsupervised technique of feature extraction.
To remove the curse of dimensionality, reduce dimension.

PCA is a technique which can transform higher dimension data to
 lower dimension data while keeping the essence of the data.
Visualization becomes easier as dimensions reduce.

blocks.t: The notes' analogy

A cameraman captures a 2-D image of a 3-D stadium at the best angle.
Information is lost — a photograph is not a stadium — but if the angle is
chosen well, everything that matters survives. PCA is the search for that best
angle, made precise: the angle that preserves the most variance.
Why Extraction, and Not Selection
From the notes
When feature selection does not help, we do feature extraction (PCA).

Normally we can simply select with domain knowledge. But if we don't have domain
knowledge, we select the feature with more data spread (variance).

blocks.cap:
The notes' worked example. Left: room varies a lot, washroom barely
 at all, so $d \gg d'$ — just keep "room" and drop the other. Middle: both
 vary comparably, $d \approx d'$, and selection has no basis for choosing.
 Right: PCA rotates the axes so that one new axis carries almost all the
 variation.

blocks.t: The notes' reasoning, step by step

items:
Suppose the columns are room and washroom. If $d \gg d'$
 — room has far more spread — choose room, because it
 distinguishes houses and washroom does not.

But what if $d \approx d'$? Both columns carry comparable
 spread and neither can be dropped without loss.

In this case we use feature extraction (PCA). It creates
 $PC_1$ and $PC_2$ — new axes — and we choose $PC_1 = \text{room}'$, as the variance is higher there.
The number of principal components is $\le n$, the number of features.

The goal is to have maximum variance while reducing dimension,
 keeping the relationships between data points intact.

blocks.t: The definition the notes arrive at

PCA finds the direction (vector) onto which projecting the data gives the
maximum variance — this is how we choose the principal components (the new
columns extracted). All PCs are orthogonal (perpendicular) to each
other.
Why variance is the right criterion

Variance is a proxy for information. A column whose values are all nearly
identical cannot distinguish one row from another — it carries no signal about
which house is which. A direction with large spread separates the data points,
and separation is what a downstream model needs.
This is a proxy, not a guarantee. See \S8 for when it fails.
The Mathematics
Step 1 — Centre the data
Let $X$ be $n\times p$. Subtract each column's mean:
\tilde X = X - \mathbf{1}\bar x^{ \top}, \qquad \bar x_j=\frac1n\sum_i X_{ij}.

Centring is mandatory. Without it the first component points from the origin
towards the data's centroid — it describes where the cloud is, not how it
varies.
Step 2 — The objective

blocks.cap:
Projecting the data onto a unit vector $u$ and measuring the variance
 of the result. Sweep $u$ through every direction and the variance traces the
 curve on the right; PCA finds its maximum.

blocks.t: Variance of a projection

For a unit vector $u\in\mathbb{R}^p$, the projection of row $\tilde x_i$ onto $u$
is the scalar $\tilde x_i^{\!\top}u$. The variance of those projections is

\operatorname{Var}(\tilde X u)
 = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(\tilde x_i^{ \top}u\right)^2
 = \frac{1}{n} u^{ \top}\tilde X^{ \top}\tilde X u
 = u^{ \top} \Sigma u ,
where
\boxed{ \Sigma = \frac{1}{n}\tilde X^{ \top}\tilde X }
is the $p\times p$ covariance matrix. So the problem is
\max_{u} u^{ \top}\Sigma u \quad\text{subject to}\quad \|u\|=1 .

The constraint is essential — without it you could scale $u$ up and make the
variance arbitrarily large.
Step 3 — Solve it: the eigenvalue problem
Lagrange multipliers
Form the Lagrangian
\mathcal{L}(u,\lambda)=u^{ \top}\Sigma u-\lambda\left(u^{ \top}u-1\right).

Differentiate and set to zero, using $\partial(u^{\!\top}\Sigma u)/\partial u = 2\Sigma u$
for symmetric $\Sigma$:

The optimal direction is an eigenvector of the covariance matrix.
Left-multiplying by $u^{\!\top}$ and using $u^{\!\top}u=1$:
u^{ \top}\Sigma u = \lambda .

The variance captured by that direction is its eigenvalue. So to
maximise the variance you take the eigenvector with the largest eigenvalue.
Everything follows from this one result

items: $PC_1$ $=$ eigenvector of $\Sigma$ with the largest eigenvalue.

$PC_2$ $=$ eigenvector with the second largest eigenvalue —
 and, because $\Sigma$ is real and symmetric, the spectral theorem
 guarantees its eigenvectors are orthogonal. That is exactly the
 notes' statement that all PCs are perpendicular to each other;
 it is not an extra constraint, it comes free.

Explained variance of component $k$ is
 $\lambda_k / \sum_j \lambda_j$.

The total variance is preserved: $\sum_k\lambda_k = \operatorname{tr}(\Sigma)$,
 the sum of the original columns' variances. PCA redistributes
 variance into fewer axes; it does not create or destroy it.

blocks.t: Step 4 — Project

Stack the top $k$ eigenvectors as columns of $W_k$ ($p\times k$). The reduced
data is
Z = \tilde X W_k \qquad (n\times k),
and the reconstruction back in the original space is
\hat X = Z W_k^{ \top} + \mathbf{1}\bar x^{ \top}.

The reconstruction error $\|\tilde X-\hat X\|_F^2 = n\sum_{j>k}\lambda_j$ —
exactly the variance you chose to discard. This is the second characterisation of
PCA: maximising retained variance is the same as minimising squared
reconstruction error.
The SVD route — what libraries actually do
Why not form $\Sigma$

Any real matrix factorises as $\tilde X = U S V^{\!\top}$ with $U,V$ orthogonal
and $S$ diagonal. Then

So the right singular vectors $V$ are the eigenvectors of $\Sigma$, and
$\lambda_k=s_k^2/n$.

Libraries use the SVD because forming $\tilde X^{\!\top}\tilde X$ squares the
condition number, losing roughly half the available precision, and because
computing a $p\times p$ matrix is wasteful when $p \gg n$ (a $10^4$-pixel image
set would need a $10^8$-entry covariance matrix). scikit-learn's PCA is a
thin wrapper around numpy.linalg.svd.
How Many Components

blocks.cap:
Left: the scree plot — eigenvalues in descending order. The
 "elbow" marks where components stop describing structure and start
 describing noise. Right: the cumulative curve, from which you read the number
 of components needed for a chosen variance threshold.

head: Rule
How it works
rows: Keep enough components for 90/95/99%. PCA(n_components=0.95) does this directly
Plot eigenvalues and cut at the bend
On standardised data, keep components with $\lambda>1$ — i.e. those explaining more than one original column would
Treat $k$ as a hyperparameter and tune it against the downstream metric. The most defensible option

blocks.t: Scaling Is Mandatory

blocks.cap:
The same two columns, with and without standardisation. Unscaled,
 PC1 is essentially the salary axis and explains 100% of the variance — not
 because salary matters more, but because it is measured in larger units.

blocks.t: PCA maximises variance, and variance has units

Variance is measured in the square of whatever unit you chose. Salary in rupees
has variance around $10^8$; age in years has variance around $10^2$. PCA will
report that salary is a million times more important — and if you re-express
salary in lakhs, the answer changes completely.

Always StandardScaler before PCA unless every column is already in
the same unit (pixel intensities, for example). Standardising makes PCA operate
on the correlation matrix rather than the covariance matrix, which is the
scale-free version of the same computation.
Limitations

head: Limitation
Consequence and remedy
rows: Maximum variance $\neq$ maximum relevance. A low-variance direction can carry all the class signal, and PCA will discard it. Use LDA when you have labels
It can only rotate. A spiral or a circle is not simplified by any rotation — use t-SNE, UMAP or a kernel PCA
"$0.4\,$age $+\,0.7\,$income $-\,0.2\,$tenure" is not something you can explain to a regulator. Use feature selection when interpretability is required
Variance is a squared quantity, so one extreme point can define PC1 entirely. Treat outliers first (Topics 28–30) or use robust PCA
The true latent factors may be correlated. Factor analysis and ICA relax this

blocks.t: PCA is a fitted transformer

The means and the eigenvectors are learned parameters. Fit on train, transform
both — never fit_transform on test, or the two sets end up in different
coordinate systems.
Code

import numpy as np
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA, KernelPCA
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.discriminant_analysis import LinearDiscriminantAnalysis
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score, GridSearchCV, train_test_split

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

# =====================================================================
# 1. PCA FROM SCRATCH -- the four steps of the derivation
# =====================================================================
n, p = 500, 4
latent = rng.normal(0, 1, (n, 2))
X = latent @ rng.normal(0, 1, (2, p)) + rng.normal(0, .35, (n, p))

# STEP 1: centre
mean = X.mean(axis=0)
Xc = X - mean

# STEP 2: covariance matrix  Sigma = (1/n) Xc' Xc
Sigma = (Xc.T @ Xc) / n
print("covariance is symmetric:", np.allclose(Sigma, Sigma.T))
print("matches numpy:", np.allclose(Sigma, np.cov(Xc, rowvar=False, bias=True)))

# STEP 3: eigendecomposition  Sigma u = lambda u
eigvals, eigvecs = np.linalg.eigh(Sigma)          # eigh: symmetric matrices
order = np.argsort(eigvals)[::-1]                 # descending
eigvals, eigvecs = eigvals[order], eigvecs[:, order]

print("\neigenvalues:", eigvals.round(4))
print("explained variance ratio:", (eigvals / eigvals.sum()).round(4))
print("sum of eigenvalues:", eigvals.sum().round(4),
      " == trace(Sigma):", np.trace(Sigma).round(4))   # variance is PRESERVED

# The variance along an eigenvector IS its eigenvalue -- verify it:
for k in range(2):
    u = eigvecs[:, k]
    print(f"  PC{k+1}: var(Xc @ u) = {np.var(Xc @ u):.6f}   lambda = {eigvals[k]:.6f}")

# Orthogonality comes FREE from the spectral theorem:
print("\nPCs are orthogonal:", np.allclose(eigvecs.T @ eigvecs, np.eye(p)))
print("PC1 . PC2 =", float(eigvecs[:, 0] @ eigvecs[:, 1]).__round__(12))

# STEP 4: project
k = 2
W = eigvecs[:, :k]
Z = Xc @ W
print("\nreduced shape:", Z.shape)

# =====================================================================
# 2. MATCHES SKLEARN
# =====================================================================
sk = PCA(n_components=k).fit(X)
print("\nsklearn explained variance ratio:", sk.explained_variance_ratio_.round(4))
print("scratch                          :", (eigvals[:k]/eigvals.sum()).round(4))
# components may differ by an overall SIGN -- that is not an error, an
# eigenvector is only defined up to sign.
for j in range(k):
    same = (np.allclose(sk.components_[j],  W[:, j], atol=1e-6) or
            np.allclose(sk.components_[j], -W[:, j], atol=1e-6))
    print(f"  component {j+1} matches (up to sign): {same}")

# =====================================================================
# 3. THE SVD ROUTE -- what libraries actually compute
# =====================================================================
U, S, Vt = np.linalg.svd(Xc, full_matrices=False)
print("\nlambda from SVD:", (S**2 / n)[:k].round(6))
print("lambda from eig:", eigvals[:k].round(6))
print("V matches eigenvectors (up to sign):",
      all(np.allclose(np.abs(Vt[j]), np.abs(eigvecs[:, j]), atol=1e-6)
          for j in range(k)))
# SVD avoids forming Xc'Xc, which would SQUARE the condition number.
print(f"cond(Xc) = {np.linalg.cond(Xc):.2e},  "
      f"cond(Xc'Xc) = {np.linalg.cond(Xc.T @ Xc):.2e}")

# =====================================================================
# 4. RECONSTRUCTION -- max variance == min squared error
# =====================================================================
X_hat = Z @ W.T + mean
err = ((X - X_hat) ** 2).sum()
print(f"\nreconstruction error {err:.4f}")
print(f"n * sum of DISCARDED eigenvalues {n * eigvals[k:].sum():.4f}")   # identical

for kk in range(1, p + 1):
    Wk = eigvecs[:, :kk]
    e = (((Xc - Xc @ Wk @ Wk.T) ** 2).sum())
    print(f"  k={kk}: retained {eigvals[:kk].sum()/eigvals.sum():6.2%}, error {e:9.4f}")

# =====================================================================
# 5. SCALING IS MANDATORY
# =====================================================================
age    = rng.normal(40, 10, 500)
salary = rng.normal(60_000, 15_000, 500) + (age - 40) * 900
raw = np.c_[age, salary]

pu = PCA().fit(raw)
ps = PCA().fit(StandardScaler().fit_transform(raw))
print(f"\nunscaled PC1 explains {pu.explained_variance_ratio_[0]:.4%}, "
      f"loadings {np.abs(pu.components_[0]).round(4)}")
print(f"scaled   PC1 explains {ps.explained_variance_ratio_[0]:.4%}, "
      f"loadings {np.abs(ps.components_[0]).round(4)}")
# Unscaled, PC1 IS the salary axis -- age's loading is ~0.0000.
print("column variances:", raw.var(axis=0).round(1))   # 1e2 vs 1e8

# =====================================================================
# 6. CHOOSING k
# =====================================================================
Xh = rng.normal(0, 1, (600, 5)) @ rng.normal(0, 1, (5, 40)) + rng.normal(0, .45, (600, 40))
Xh = StandardScaler().fit_transform(Xh)
full = PCA().fit(Xh)
cum = np.cumsum(full.explained_variance_ratio_)
for lvl in [.90, .95, .99]:
    print(f"{lvl:.0%} of variance needs {np.searchsorted(cum, lvl)+1} of 40 components")

# Kaiser criterion on standardised data: keep lambda > 1
print("Kaiser (lambda > 1):", int((full.explained_variance_ > 1).sum()), "components")

# Or let sklearn hit a variance target directly:
print("PCA(n_components=0.95) picks:",
      PCA(n_components=0.95).fit(Xh).n_components_)

# =====================================================================
# 7. IT IS UNSUPERVISED -- variance is NOT relevance
# =====================================================================
n2 = 800
signal = rng.normal(0, 1, n2)                    # LOW variance, ALL the signal
noise  = rng.normal(0, 12, (n2, 9))              # HIGH variance, no signal
X2 = np.c_[signal, noise]
y2 = (signal > 0).astype(int)

base = cross_val_score(LogisticRegression(max_iter=800), X2, y2, cv=5).mean()
pca1 = cross_val_score(make_pipeline(PCA(n_components=1),
                                     LogisticRegression(max_iter=800)),
                       X2, y2, cv=5).mean()
lda1 = cross_val_score(make_pipeline(LinearDiscriminantAnalysis(n_components=1),
                                     LogisticRegression(max_iter=800)),
                       X2, y2, cv=5).mean()
print(f"\nall 10 features {base:.3f} | PCA 1 comp {pca1:.3f} | LDA 1 comp {lda1:.3f}")
# PCA throws the signal away: the informative direction has the SMALLEST
# variance. LDA, which uses the labels, keeps it. This is PCA's core limitation.

# =====================================================================
# 8. IT IS LINEAR -- a rotation cannot unroll a circle
# =====================================================================
t = rng.uniform(0, 2*np.pi, 600)
r = np.r_[rng.normal(1, .08, 300), rng.normal(3, .08, 300)]
circles = np.c_[r*np.cos(t), r*np.sin(t)]
y3 = (r > 2).astype(int)

lin = cross_val_score(make_pipeline(PCA(n_components=1),
                                    LogisticRegression()), circles, y3, cv=5).mean()
ker = cross_val_score(make_pipeline(KernelPCA(n_components=1, kernel="rbf", gamma=1.0),
                                    LogisticRegression()), circles, y3, cv=5).mean()
print(f"\nconcentric circles: PCA {lin:.3f}   KernelPCA(rbf) {ker:.3f}")

# =====================================================================
# 9. IN A PIPELINE -- scale, reduce, model; k tuned by CV
# =====================================================================
y4 = (Xh[:, :3].sum(axis=1) + rng.normal(0, .8, 600) > 0).astype(int)
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(Xh, y4, test_size=.25, random_state=0)

gs = GridSearchCV(
    make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), PCA(), LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000)),
    {"pca__n_components": [2, 5, 10, 20, 30]},
    cv=5, scoring="roc_auc", n_jobs=-1).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
print("\nbest k:", gs.best_params_, round(gs.best_score_, 4))
print("test auc:", round(gs.score(X_te, y_te), 4))

# The transform is FITTED -- means and eigenvectors are learned from train:
fitted = gs.best_estimator_.named_steps["pca"]
print("stored mean (first 4):", fitted.mean_[:4].round(3))
print("components shape:", fitted.components_.shape)
# Applied UNCHANGED to test and production. Never fit_transform on test.
Summary
Everything on one page

items:
PCA is an unsupervised feature-extraction technique that
 transforms higher-dimensional data to lower-dimensional data
 while keeping the essence of the data. It removes the curse of
 dimensionality and makes visualization easier.

When feature selection does not help, we do feature
 extraction. If one column has far more spread ($d\gg d'$), just select
 it. If $d\approx d'$, selection cannot choose — so PCA builds new axes.

PCA finds the direction onto which projecting the data gives the
 maximum variance. All PCs are orthogonal to each other. The
 number of PCs is $\le$ the number of features.

The mathematics: centre the data, form
 $\Sigma=\frac1n\tilde X^{\!\top}\tilde X$, and solve
 $\max_u u^{\!\top}\Sigma u$ s.t. $\|u\|=1$. Lagrange multipliers give
 $\Sigma u=\lambda u$ — the components are the eigenvectors of
 the covariance matrix, and the variance each captures is its
 eigenvalue.

Orthogonality is free: $\Sigma$ is symmetric, so the spectral theorem
 guarantees it.

Explained variance ratio $=\lambda_k/\sum\lambda_j$. Total variance is
 preserved; PCA redistributes it.

Maximising retained variance $\equiv$ minimising squared reconstruction
 error.

Libraries use the SVD of $\tilde X$, not the eigendecomposition
 of $\Sigma$ — better conditioning, and cheaper when $p\gg n$.

Choose $k$ by cumulative variance (90/95/99%), the scree elbow, the
 Kaiser criterion, or cross-validation.
Scaling is mandatory — variance has units.

Limitations: unsupervised (use LDA with labels), linear (use t-SNE or
 kernel PCA), uninterpretable components, sensitive to outliers.

blocks.t: Questions you will actually be asked
Q. Explain PCA in one minute.

Centre the data, compute the covariance matrix, and take its eigenvectors. The
eigenvector with the largest eigenvalue is the direction of greatest variance —
the first principal component — and its eigenvalue is the variance it captures.
Project onto the top $k$ eigenvectors to reduce from $p$ dimensions to $k$ while
keeping as much variance as possible.
Q. Why are the principal components orthogonal?

Because the covariance matrix is real and symmetric, and the spectral theorem
guarantees such a matrix has an orthogonal eigenbasis. Orthogonality is not an
extra constraint imposed on the optimisation — it falls out of it.
Q. Why must you scale before PCA?

Because PCA maximises variance and variance carries the square of the unit.
Salary in rupees has variance around $10^8$, age in years around $10^2$, so PC1
would be the salary axis regardless of relevance — and re-expressing salary in
lakhs would change the answer.
Q. Can PCA hurt a supervised model?

Yes. It is unsupervised, so it maximises variance rather than class separation.
If the discriminative direction happens to have small variance — a low-variance
signal buried among high-variance noise — PCA discards exactly the component you
needed. LDA, which uses the labels, is the supervised alternative.
Q. How do you choose the number of components?

Cumulative explained variance against a threshold (typically 95%), the elbow of
the scree plot, the Kaiser criterion ($\lambda>1$ on standardised data), or — the
most defensible — treat $k$ as a hyperparameter and tune it against the
downstream metric by cross-validation.
Q. Why do libraries use SVD rather than eigendecomposition?

Forming $X^{\!\top}X$ squares the condition number, losing about half the
available precision, and building a $p\times p$ matrix is wasteful when $p\gg n$.
The SVD of $X$ gives the same eigenvectors directly, with $\lambda_k=s_k^2/n$.
Q. Your data lies on two concentric circles. Will PCA separate them?

No. PCA can only rotate, and no rotation makes concentric circles linearly
separable. You need a non-linear method — kernel PCA with an RBF kernel, t-SNE,
or UMAP.
